item.text: {"chapter_id":"4B","answers":[{"question_id":"4B.1","answer":"Mexico retained competitive multiparty elections, realistic alternation, and generally free and fair administration, and opposition mobilization and judicial review remained effective in 2023. These were important inherited and institutional constraints rather than clear evidence of López Obrador’s voluntary self-binding. Conversely, he proposed and backed Plan B, which would have reduced INE powers, budget, staffing, professional capacity, affirmative-action structures, and local administration; the Supreme Court and INE suspended or invalidated it, while the June 2023 local elections proceeded under the prior rules. The evidence therefore shows continued contestability despite ruler-attributable attempts that threatened electoral independence, with no 2023 opposition victory accepted by López Obrador personally as a defining test.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E017","BATCH-0003-E018","BATCH-0004-E015","BATCH-0005-E008","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0040-E003","BATCH-0043-E010","BATCH-0051-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E016","BATCH-0012-E013","BATCH-0012-E015","BATCH-0042-E006","BATCH-0048-E006","BATCH-0045-E001","BATCH-0030-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most evidence concerns the 2022-2023 reform conflict rather than a completed national transfer of power.","The index does not provide a verified 2023 national opposition victory or direct evidence of López Obrador’s conduct after final judicial invalidation."]},{"question_id":"4B.2","answer":"The record is predominantly adverse. López Obrador proposed or supported electoral changes that would weaken INE autonomy, advocated military control of the National Guard despite its constitutional civilian design, pursued secrecy and national-security treatment for major projects, and criticized courts and critics when they constrained his agenda. Budget and appointment pressure affected INAI, INE, the judiciary, regulators, and audit-related institutions. Some proposals were blocked, suspended, or invalidated by courts, and some institutional rules remained formally protective; those constraints qualify the outcome but do not convert the ruler-attributable conduct into restraint. Evidence of personal intent to secure continued office is sometimes inferential, especially because López Obrador could not constitutionally be reelected.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0013-E016","BATCH-0013-E017","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0014-E017","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0031-E004","BATCH-0043-E006","BATCH-0043-E007","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0055-E007","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0047-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E005","BATCH-0005-E010","BATCH-0010-E005","BATCH-0040-E003","BATCH-0043-E010","BATCH-0055-E012","BATCH-0055-E013"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Several measures were proposals rather than implemented law.","The evidence establishes institutional pressure and erosion more clearly than a proven personal plan for indefinite reelection."]},{"question_id":"4B.3","answer":"Formal protections for speech, assembly, association, and civil society remained in place, independent media operated, internet access was not generally blocked, and demonstrations against Plan B occurred at scale. There were also some cooperation mechanisms, legal reforms, and institutional initiatives. In practice, however, López Obrador repeatedly stigmatized journalists, NGOs, feminists, defenders, judges, and critics through presidential briefings and targeted accusations; documented press attacks, threats, killings, self-censorship, protest criminalization, disproportionate force, and weak protection and investigation persisted. The administration’s public rhetoric and failure to remedy impunity are attributable at the executive level, while many physical attacks were committed by criminal, state, or local actors whose individual causal links to the president are not established.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0015-E018","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0052-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E012","BATCH-0004-E005","BATCH-0012-E007","BATCH-0012-E008","BATCH-0012-E009","BATCH-0014-E008","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0041-E006","BATCH-0051-E008","BATCH-0026-E016"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide a complete national account of remedies for every 2023 violation.","Criminal violence and local-government conduct complicate direct presidential attribution for individual attacks."]},{"question_id":"4B.4","answer":"Independent courts and electoral institutions exercised meaningful constraint: the Supreme Court invalidated the National Guard transfer and Plan B provisions, and courts ordered or enabled action concerning autonomous regulators. The government also invited and cooperated with a UN detention visit, and formal legal safeguards remained. Against this, López Obrador publicly attacked courts, supported or enacted measures transferring civilian authority to the military, failed to fill or vetoed appointments affecting INAI and regulators, left INAI unable to function fully, and did not promptly demonstrate compliance with the National Guard judgment. Military obstruction of Ayotzinapa, weak civilian oversight, transparency failures, and pressure on judges show that formal checks survived but operated under substantial executive and administrative pressure.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E009","BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0009-E001","BATCH-0010-E005","BATCH-0014-E002","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0043-E010","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0049-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E015","BATCH-0013-E004","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0041-E008","BATCH-0055-E004","BATCH-0055-E012","BATCH-0057-E007","BATCH-0057-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index often reports institutional conditions rather than a complete record of executive compliance after rulings.","Some appointment blockages involved the Senate or autonomous institutions, so personal presidential control is not uniform."]},{"question_id":"4B.5","answer":"The administration expanded military personnel and command into public security, infrastructure, ports, customs, migration, and other civilian functions, while analysts describe loyalty, centralization, and political alignment as more important than neutral professional administration. Military jurisdiction, weak civilian oversight, opaque detention practices, delayed autonomous-agency appointments, and alleged influence by presidential relatives reinforce concerns about politicization and institutional capture. Counterevidence includes formal civil-service and constitutional safeguards, some judicially compelled appointments, CNDH self-reported internal controls, and the absence of proof that López Obrador personally directed every appointment or abuse. Overall, the period shows substantial institutional militarization and politicization, with attribution strongest for the policy direction and weaker for individual personnel decisions.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E008","BATCH-0013-E012","BATCH-0013-E017","BATCH-0026-E006","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0031-E013","BATCH-0048-E012","BATCH-0055-E009","BATCH-0055-E010","BATCH-0055-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-R01-E005","BATCH-0014-E002","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0055-E003","BATCH-0055-E004","BATCH-0057-E002"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index lacks a complete appointment-by-appointment personnel audit.","Some evidence is analytical or advocacy-based and does not establish the qualifications or motives of every appointee."]},{"question_id":"4B.6","answer":"Independent media, internet access, and formal press and information rights continued to exist, and online political mobilization remained robust. However, López Obrador and officials used recurring stigmatizing rhetoric and public briefings to discredit journalists and critics; government advertising was concentrated among a limited group of outlets; information requests and INAI capacity deteriorated; military and infrastructure secrecy increased; and surveillance allegations were denied or minimized rather than transparently resolved. Criminal violence was a major external source of pressure, but the administration’s rhetoric, resource allocation, transparency restrictions, and failure to remedy impunity were ruler- or government-attributable contributors. Proposed cybersecurity restrictions and content controls were serious risks but were not all enacted.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0026-E013","BATCH-0026-E015","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0044-E012","BATCH-0051-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0026-E015","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0057-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Some quantitative press-violence evidence covers 2022 or mixed periods.","Advertising concentration does not alone prove content control, and surveillance attribution is often investigative rather than finally adjudicated."]},{"question_id":"4B.7","answer":"There were meaningful inclusive developments: same-sex marriage became nationwide, gender recognition and disability-rights reforms advanced, gender quotas produced near parity in Congress, and some protections for migrants and other groups expanded. The administration also supported social programs and some legal and international human-rights measures. Conversely, Indigenous and Afro-Mexican groups remained underrepresented, Plan B threatened affirmative-action and local electoral structures, barriers to abortion and disability inclusion persisted, and Indigenous people, migrants, women, LGBT+ people, defenders, and opposition regions experienced discrimination, insecurity, or unequal access. Some reforms were enacted by courts, Congress, or autonomous institutions rather than personally by López Obrador, so credit and causation are mixed.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0003-E018","BATCH-0004-E015","BATCH-0005-E008","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0052-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0004-E012","BATCH-0005-E008","BATCH-0013-E016","BATCH-0045-E001","BATCH-0048-E006","BATCH-0048-E011","BATCH-0049-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index provides limited direct measurement of implementation disparities across regions and groups.","Many positive legal changes are not shown to be presidential initiatives or uniformly enforced."]},{"question_id":"4B.8","answer":"The constitutional six-year term and nonreelection rule remained in force, and López Obrador did not obtain a second presidential term. Elections and succession planning proceeded within constitutional structures, and courts and electoral institutions constrained reform efforts. Nevertheless, he used his political authority and Morena’s succession process to preserve influence, promoted internal succession arrangements, and supported reforms affecting electoral and judicial institutions. Historical evidence also shows that he previously rejected adverse electoral rulings in 2006 and 2012, which qualifies—but does not directly determine—the 2023 record. The 2023 evidence therefore supports formal compliance with the term limit but mixed respect for the broader spirit of neutral succession and institutional transfer.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E017","BATCH-0026-E009","BATCH-0028-E006","BATCH-0031-E004","BATCH-0031-E012","BATCH-0029-E008","BATCH-0042-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0024-E004","BATCH-0024-E006","BATCH-0013-E016","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0043-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index contains limited direct evidence of the 2024 transfer itself because the target period ends in 2023.","Historical rejection of electoral rulings is relevant context but not direct evidence of 2023 succession conduct."]},{"question_id":"4B.9","answer":"Formal safeguards existed: communications interception generally required judicial authorization, courts invalidated an inadequately bounded undercover-operation power, internet blocking was not nationwide, and some courts protected privacy and access rights. At the same time, military and security agencies were linked by investigative evidence to Pegasus surveillance of journalists, defenders, investigators, and officials; legal authority and judicial authorization were disputed or absent, INAI orders were not promptly obeyed, detention records were underregistered, and the government denied or minimized the allegations without showing completed accountability. Metadata retention, geolocation powers, proposed biometric and cybersecurity measures, and military intelligence structures created additional risks. The evidence supports a mixed formal framework but adverse operational oversight and remedy.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0014-E007","BATCH-0026-E015","BATCH-0026-E019","BATCH-0057-E006","BATCH-0057-E007","BATCH-0057-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E005","BATCH-0010-E001","BATCH-0030-E002","BATCH-0042-E010","BATCH-0055-E012","BATCH-0057-E005","BATCH-0057-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No evidence proves López Obrador personally ordered each surveillance operation.","Several surveillance findings rely on leaks, forensic investigations, or advocacy reports, and final accountability outcomes are incomplete."]},{"question_id":"4B.10","answer":"The end-of-period trajectory is mixed but predominantly erosive. Democratic resilience remained real because elections stayed competitive, opposition and civil society mobilized, courts invalidated major executive-backed measures, the INE operated under prior rules, and some rights and accountability initiatives advanced. These strengths were substantially institutional or societal and cannot be credited wholly to López Obrador. His attributable legacy included expanded military control of civilian functions, weakened or impaired autonomous oversight, pressure on courts and media, transparency deterioration, surveillance concerns, persistent impunity, and incomplete remedies for Ayotzinapa and journalist or defender violence. Positive social and legal reforms, UN cooperation, and some judicial corrections qualify the assessment, but they do not establish that political freedom was durably stronger through enacted, ruler-led, independently reviewable institutions.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E002","BATCH-0003-E017","BATCH-0003-E018","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0043-E010","BATCH-0051-E019","BATCH-0051-E013","BATCH-0049-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0013-E004","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0052-E011","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0057-E017","BATCH-0004-E015"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index mixes direct 2023 evidence with retrospective, baseline, and post-period assessments.","There is no single independent before-and-after measure isolating López Obrador’s contribution to democratic resilience, and several outcomes reflect courts, Congress, civil society, criminal actors, or inherited conditions."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The strongest adverse pattern is ruler-attributable institutional pressure: electoral administration, autonomous oversight, civilian security control, transparency, courts, media rhetoric, and surveillance accountability.","The strongest qualifying pattern is institutional resilience: courts, INE, civil society, opposition mobilization, and formal constitutional safeguards continued to constrain executive action.","Formal laws and institutions often remained protective while implementation, administrative compliance, transparency, and remedies were weaker.","Attribution is strongest for López Obrador’s proposals, public rhetoric, executive sponsorship, and policy direction; it is weaker for individual abuses, criminal violence, local-government conduct, and decisions formally made by Congress or autonomous institutions.","The evidence is concentrated on 2022-2023 institutional and rights conditions, with limited direct evidence of the eventual constitutional transfer at the end of the ruler-period."]}
